title: Chardi kala as philosophy
hookLine: a settled optimism rooted in trust, not in circumstances
last: KAAM: NOT KILLED, NOT CROWNED, KEPT.

cards: The email that says no. The test result. The car that won't start in the rain.

A setback lands, and there's a phrase for how Sikhs try to meet it, a phrase that closes the Ardas, the standing prayer: chardi kala. Rising spirits. It showed up early on this path as hope that keeps getting up.
Today it isn't a mood. It's a way of seeing the world, with roots that go down below the weather.

teach.b: First, the line. The Ardas closes with these words: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. In paraphrase: Nanak, with the Name, rising spirits; by your will, the good of all.
Look at what chardi kala stands next to. Not good news. Not a lucky break.
Naam, the Name. The rising is rooted.
Second, roots, not circumstances. Ordinary cheer climbs and falls with the forecast. Chardi kala, as Sikhs describe it, rests on trust in the One, so it doesn't need the forecast to cooperate.
A tree on a windy hill bends hard in a storm. It stays because of what's underground.
Third, it doesn't pretend. Earlier in this stretch, the Gurus called pain a medicine, without ever pretending it isn't pain. Chardi kala doesn't deny the setback.
It simply refuses to let the setback write the ending.

teach.h: RISING FOR THE GOOD OF ALL.
teach.b: Grief and rising spirits can sit in the same person on the same afternoon. Fourth, it faces outward. The line doesn't end with my spirits.
It ends with sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

In Sikh thought, rising spirits are meant to be shared. The one in chardi kala can be the one others lean on in a hard room: steady voice, warm tea, a joke at the right moment. Not because things are fine.

how: Sikhs close the Ardas with the words 'Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala', and speak of chardi kala as a settled, rising spirit grounded in trust in Waheguru rather than in how things are going.

games.q: what does “chardi kala as philosophy” mean?
o: a brave face that hides how hard things are
rising spirits rooted in trust, not in good news
cheerfulness that depends on how the day goes

p: the Name the rising is rooted in
climbs and falls with the forecast

s: chardi kala means pretending everything is fine
it doesn't deny the setback; it refuses to let it write the ending.
in the Ardas, chardi kala comes right after naam
nanak naam chardi kala: the rising is rooted in the Name.
the Ardas line ends with the good of all

games.q: bad news lands at work and the room goes quiet. what does chardi kala look like?
o: name it honestly, then help steady the room.
make sure everyone knows how bad it is.
games.why: chardi kala doesn't pretend; it's rooted in trust and faces outward, toward the good of all.

practice: Bring to mind one setback from this week, small or not so small, and notice where it sits in your body.

Breathe in and picture roots going down from where you sit, into ground the setback can't reach; breathe out and let the corners of your mouth lift a little, not because it's fine, but because you're still standing.
If you pray, say the Ardas's closing words quietly: Nanak naam chardi kala.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala as philosophy. Rising spirits, rooted in the Name and in trust, not in circumstances, and turned toward the good of all. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rising spirits; the phrase that closes the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: rising, rooted. Bent by the storm, held by what's underground. See you tomorrow.
